This repo provides python scripts to replicate the calculations in the paper "Surprising payouts of parimutuel numbers games"

This code is provided under GPL v3.0.

# List of files

   * bootstrap-chisq.py = Bootstrap estimate of chi^2 divergence.  This code was generated by Claude Fable.
   * kentucky-data-compare.py = Bisect the KY data and compare plug-in chi^2 divergence of the two halves
   * payouts-per-year.py = Subdivide the MA or NJ data into fiscal years and calculate average payouts, standard erorr, and confidence intervals.  The resulting data can be used to generate Figure 1 in the paper.
   * simulate.py = The workhorse code, it simulates numbers game drawings.  This file includes code to generate data used for multiple figures in the paper.

# How to reconstruct the figures and information reported in the paper

The scripts expect a root directory that contains the following
subdirectories:
   * NJ data set
   * MA data set
   * CA data set
   * a subdirectory with the python scripts; the name of this subdirectory doesn't matter
The first three directories correspond to the data set available on Zenodo as DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23201089

## Figure 1

To construct this figure, you need to know the average straight payout for the New Jersey game by fiscal year.  This information can be extracted using Excel or other spreadsheet program from NJ data set/NJ-pick-3.csv or is printed to the screen by payouts-per-year.py.

## Figure 2

The function figure2() in simulate.py generates a CSV file figure2.csv of pairs (N, payout).  For each N, it computes the expected payout by simulating many drawings and taking the average of the resulting payouts.  Because the game only involves straight tickets and gamblers bet uniformly at random, the python for this is very short.  This data can then be read in to Mathematica and the plot generated using the ListLogLinear function.

## Table 2

The data that needs to be verified are the chi^2 values, which are verified via assertion statements in the function test_chi_mq_straight() in simulate.py.  This can be run by hand, or it is run via "pytest simulate.py".

## Figures 3 and 4

These are drawn using Mathematica from the files KY data set/KY-wagers.csv and CA data set/CA-wagers-straight.csv.  

For Figure 3, apply the ListPlot function with Joined -> True.

For Figure 4, use ListLogPlot with Joined -> True.

## California convex combination

It is asserted that California and the convex combination with parameter 0.277 have the same value for chi^2(m||q).  This is verified in test_chi_mq_CA() in simulate.py.

## Bootstrap sampling of chi^2(m q)

Done using bootstrap-chimq.py.

## Figure 5

The data is generated by verify_companion_result2() in simulate.py, which creates a file simulation-straight.csv.

## Figure 6

Generate the data for the plot using the function generate_contour() in simulate.py, which creates a file contours.csv.  Mathematica can then produce the figure from that data.

## Rados convex combination

The fact that the convex combination with x about 0.31 has the same chi^2(q||m) as Rados, and the fact that this convex combination has chi^2(m||q) of about 0.14, is verified in test_rados() in simulate.py.

The function test_rados_range() checks the claim on chi^2(m||q) for 26%-36% convex combinations.

# Simulations and random seeds

The data that is generated by simulations (Figures 2, 5, and 6, giving figure2.csv, simulation-straight.csv, and contours.csv) was generated via the function generate_data_sets(), which calls figure2(), verify_companion_result2(), generate_contour(), and figure6_corners() with a fixed random seed.
